definition: A system that keeps a history of every change made to a set of files, so you can see what changed, who changed it, when, and go back to any earlier version.

In Git, "distributed" means every single clone of a project holds the entire history, not just the latest files — so you can commit, browse history, and work fully offline, and there's no one machine whose loss wipes out the project.
A repository (or "repo") is a project's full folder of files plus its entire saved history of commits, all tracked together by Git.
The actual files on your disk as you see and edit them right now — this is where you make changes before Git knows anything about them.
A holding area where you place the specific changes you want in your next commit, using git add — it lets you build a commit out of only some of your edits rather than all of them at once.

The command used to set Git's own settings — most importantly your name and email, which get attached to every commit you make. E.g. git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace" tells Git whose name to record.
The command that turns an ordinary folder into a Git repository by creating a hidden .git folder inside it — it doesn't touch, delete, or rename any of your existing files.
The command that downloads a full copy of a remote repository — including its entire commit history, not just a snapshot — onto your own machine.
The name Git gives by default to the remote repository you cloned from or first connected to — it's just a nickname, not a special technical requirement.
The command that moves a change from your Working Directory into the Staging Area, marking it as ready to be included in your next commit.
The command that reports which files are staged, which are changed but unstaged, and which are untracked — it only reports information and never modifies any of your files.
The command that permanently saves everything currently in the Staging Area as a new snapshot in the repository's history.
A commit-message writing style that reads like a command being given right now — e.g. "Fix login bug" instead of "Fixed login bug" or "Fixing login bug."
The command that lists your commit history, newest commit first, showing details like the author and date for each one.
The command that shows your unstaged changes line by line, comparing your current files against your last commit.
The command used to undo changes — git restore file.txt discards unstaged edits back to the last commit, while git restore --staged file.txt unstages a file without touching your edits.
A command that replaces your most recent commit instead of creating a new one — it can update the commit message, the staged changes, or both at once.
A command that undoes the changes from an earlier commit by creating a brand-new commit that reverses them — the original commit stays in history, which makes it safe to use even after pushing.
A command that moves your current branch's pointer to an earlier commit, effectively rewinding it — how it treats your uncommitted changes depends on the mode (--soft, --mixed, or --hard).
A movable label that points at one specific commit — not a copy of your files. As you commit, the branch label automatically moves forward to point at your newest commit.
The modern command for moving onto a different existing branch, which also updates your working files to match that branch.
The older, more multi-purpose command that (among other things) can switch you onto a different branch — largely replaced today by the more focused git switch and git restore.
The command that combines the commits from another branch into your current branch, creating a single unified history.

A merge where your current branch hasn't diverged from the branch being merged in, so Git can simply slide your branch pointer forward — no new merge commit is needed. E.g. you branched off main and only main's branch moved on with your new commits; merging back in is just catching main's pointer up to yours.

A merge that happens when both branches have new commits since they split apart, so Git combines both histories into one new commit with two parent commits. E.g. you and a teammate both added commits to your own branches since they diverged from main — merging needs a real combining commit, not just a pointer move.

What happens when two branches being merged changed the same lines of a file in different ways — Git can't guess which version you want, so it pauses and marks the conflicting spot in the file itself, wrapping both versions between <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers with a ======= line splitting them, for you to edit by hand into what the file should actually say.
A command that replays your branch's commits one by one on top of another branch's latest commit, producing a straight-line history instead of a merge commit.
Running git rebase with the -i flag, which opens an editable list of your recent commits so you can reorder, reword, or squash them together before they're replayed.
Combining several separate commits into one single commit, usually done during an interactive rebase to tidy up messy history before sharing it.
A version of your repository that lives somewhere else — usually on a server like GitHub — that your local repository can push commits to or pull commits from.
The command that uploads your local commits to a remote repository so others can see them.
The command that downloads new commits from a remote repository and immediately merges them into your current branch — it's really git fetch followed by git merge.
The command that downloads new commits from a remote repository without touching your current branch at all — the safer, quieter alternative to git pull when you just want to look first.
A local branch that's linked to a matching branch on a remote, so commands like git push and git pull know which remote branch to talk to without you naming it every time.
Your own personal hosted copy of someone else's repository (typically on GitHub), which you can freely experiment on without affecting the original project.
A request you open on GitHub (or similar) asking a project's maintainer to review and merge changes from your branch or fork into their repository.
A workflow where everyone merges small changes into the main branch constantly, rather than working for a long time on separate long-lived branches.

A branching strategy built around long-lived branches for scheduled releases, alongside separate feature and hotfix branches — heavier than trunk-based development but structured for planned release cycles.
A branch created to isolate the work for just one specific change or feature, kept separate from main until that work is ready to merge in.

A command that deletes untracked files (files Git isn't tracking at all) from your Working Directory — running it with -n first previews what would be deleted, and -f actually deletes it; it never touches tracked files.
A flag on git log that searches your commit history for commits which added or removed a specific piece of text, instead of you having to scroll through everything by hand.
A command that shows which commit (and who) last changed every single line of a file — meant for finding context on a change, not for pointing fingers.
A tool that helps you find the exact commit that introduced a bug by testing the midpoint between a known-good and known-bad commit and narrowing the search in half each time.
A command that permanently marks one specific commit with a memorable name, most often used to mark release versions like v2.0.

A command that temporarily sets aside your uncommitted changes so you get a clean Working Directory — useful when you need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit yet. git stash pop brings those changes back.
A command that copies just one specific commit from another branch onto your current branch, without bringing along any of that branch's other commits.
A local log recording everywhere your branches have pointed, even after commits become unreachable through commands like git reset — it acts as a safety net for recovering "lost" commits.

A whole separate Git repository embedded inside another one, with the parent repo locking in one exact commit of it rather than tracking its ongoing history — e.g. pulling a shared UI-component library into your app's repo as a submodule instead of copy-pasting its files in.

Short for Git Large File Storage — an extension that replaces large files (like videos) with small pointer files in your normal history, storing the actual heavy content separately so the repository stays fast.
In Git's internal object model, the object type that stores a file's raw contents — it doesn't even store the filename, just the data.
In Git's internal object model, the object type that stores a folder's structure — which files and subfolders it contains and what they're named.
A pointer to the commit you currently have checked out, usually via the branch you are on.
The hidden folder at the top of a repository that holds all of its history and settings.
Secure Hash Algorithm: the hash function Git uses to give each commit a unique ID.
Version control system: a tool that records changes to files over time, such as Git.
Git Large File Storage: an extension that keeps big files outside the normal repository history.
A website that hosts Git repositories and adds code review and automation.
Uniform resource locator: the web address of a page or a remote repository.
Makes `git diff` show only the changes already staged for the next commit.
Makes `git config` apply a setting to every repository of the current user.
Makes `git config` apply a setting to the current repository only.
The Git setting that holds the name recorded on your commits.
The Git setting that holds the email recorded on your commits.
The flag that gives a commit its message on the command line, as in `git commit -m "message"`.
The flag that makes `git commit` stage every modified tracked file first.
Replaces the most recent commit with a new one, so you can fix its message or contents.
Shows extra detail, such as the full diff inside the commit message editor.
Makes `git log` print each commit on a single line.
Limits `git log` to the given number of most recent commits.
Makes `git log` list commits that add or remove the given text.
Makes `git log` list commits whose message matches a pattern.
Makes `git reset` move the branch only, keeping your changes staged.
Makes `git reset` move the branch and unstage changes, keeping the files as they are.
Makes `git reset` move the branch and also overwrite your files, discarding changes.
Makes `git switch` create a new branch and switch to it.
Makes `git checkout` create a new branch and switch to it.
Makes `git rebase` open an interactive list of commits you can reorder, edit or squash.
Forces the push, replacing the remote branch even if that discards commits.
A safer force push that fails if someone else has pushed to the branch since you last fetched.
Shows what a command would do without actually doing it.
Shows more detail, such as the commit each branch points at.
The git config flag that writes a setting for every user on the machine.
A flag that applies a command to every branch, ref or file instead of just the current one.
The git log and diff flag that summarises which files changed and by how many lines.
A git merge flag that adds one-line summaries of the merged commits to the merge message.
A flag that makes Git carry out a command even when it would normally refuse for safety.
Not a real option of git commit; the correct flag for changing the last commit is --amend.
Not a real option of git commit; it is a made-up flag, unlike the real --amend.
A flag that does not open the interactive commit list in git rebase; -i does that.
A file at the top of a project that explains what it is and how to use it.
Not the git log option for searching changes; the real pickaxe search flag is -S.
The safer git push option --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite work you have not seen.
The hyphenated form of version control: a system that records every change to files over time.
Storage for a project's files together with their complete change history.
Lightweight movable pointers to commits that let you work on separate lines of development.
Local branches that are linked to a remote branch so push and pull know where to go.
Copying someone else's repository to your own account so you can change it freely.
Git objects that store the contents of a single file.
Git objects that store a folder's structure by listing its files and subfolders.
